summary: Describes the multicast routing architectures deployed on the Internet and briefly points to their specifications. It also reclassifies several older RFCs as Historic because the protocols were never widely deployed or fell out of use. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a guided tour of how multicast routing works on the Internet. It also retires some old protocols nobody uses anymore.

questions: how does multicast routing work on the internet
what happened to mospf and bgmp
what is a rendezvous point in multicast
subtitle: A guided tour of how the Internet routes multicast traffic to many destinations at once.

tldr.problem: The Internet needs ways to send data from one source to multiple receivers efficiently. Several multicast routing protocols were invented, but only some became widely deployed.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5110 describes the deployed multicast routing architectures, including PIM-SM (the dominant protocol), PIM-DM, DVMRP, and others. It covers forwarding state setup, topology distribution, source discovery, rendezvous point configuration, redundancy, host interaction, and flooding reduction.
tldr.outcome: PIM-SM is the only multicast routing protocol deployed in both intra-domain and inter-domain networks. Several older protocols (MOSPF, CBT, BGMP) have been reclassified as Historic due to lack of deployment.

today: RFC 5110 is Informational. It describes the multicast routing landscape as of 2008. PIM-SM remains the dominant multicast routing protocol deployed globally. Three older protocols (MOSPF, CBT, BGMP) are now Historic, reflecting their lack of deployment or obsolescence.

sections.title: Multicast Routing Overview
sections.content:
Multicast is the ability to send data from one source to a group of receivers efficiently, without sending duplicate copies to each receiver. To route multicast packets, routers need to set up forwarding state for each multicast group, learn which hosts want to receive which groups, and distribute topology information so packets reach the right place.

RFC 5110 describes the multicast routing architectures currently deployed on the Internet. It covers seven classes of mechanisms: setting up multicast forwarding state (which routing protocol to use), distributing multicast topology information, learning active sources, configuring rendezvous points, redundancy mechanisms, host interaction, and link-layer flooding reduction.

The RFC also reclassifies three older protocols to Historic status: MOSPF, CBT, and BGMP. These protocols were never widely deployed or have fallen out of use.
sections.eli5: When a host wants to receive a multicast group, it tells its local router. The router sets up a tree of paths through the network so packets from the source reach everyone who joined, but nobody else gets flooded. This document describes how routers do that.

sections.title: Multicast Forwarding Protocols
sections.content:
PIM-SM (Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode) is the dominant multicast routing protocol. It assumes most subnets do not have receivers for a given group, so it builds a distribution tree rooted at a rendezvous point (RP) where sources register. When receivers join, a tree is built on-demand from the RP to them. Later, the network can optimize by building (source, group)-specific trees. PIM-SM works in both intra-domain and inter-domain networks.

PIM-DM (Dense Mode) floods multicast throughout the network and prunes branches that do not want the traffic. It works best in small networks where most subnets have receivers. It is no longer in widespread use, having been superseded by PIM-SM.

Bidirectional PIM establishes a shared tree for all sources for a single group root. It does not switch to shortest-path trees and does not have data-driven events, making it simpler than PIM-SM in some sites with many sources.

DVMRP (Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol) was the first multicast protocol and included tunneling to interconnect multicast islands. It has been almost entirely replaced by PIM-SM; only legacy deployments remain.

MOSPF, CBT, and BGMP are now Historic. MOSPF required OSPF and did not scale to inter-domain use. CBT was an academic project that never saw production use. BGMP never gained vendor support.
sections.eli5: PIM-Sparse Mode is the main protocol. It builds a tree from a rendezvous point to the receivers. Dense Mode floods and prunes. Bidirectional PIM shares a tree for all sources. Others like DVMRP, MOSPF, CBT, and BGMP are retired or nearly retired.

sections.title: Distributing Topology Information
sections.content:
PIM is topology-independent: it can use unicast routing information to build multicast trees. However, in some networks, multicast topology should differ from unicast topology (for example, to exclude certain paths from multicast).

Multiprotocol BGP (MBGP, RFC 4760) extends BGP to advertise separate multicast reachability information using address family identifiers. SAFI=1 is unicast, SAFI=2 is multicast. Multiprotocol BGP is widely deployed wherever BGP is used and is essential for inter-domain multicast.

OSPF and IS-IS Multi-Topology Extensions allow interior gateway protocols to distribute separate multicast topology information for intra-domain routing. These are less commonly used than MBGP.

When some routers advertise multicast routes and others do not, implementations may first check the multicast routing table, then fall back to the unicast table if no match is found.
sections.eli5: Routers need to know the shape of the multicast network. BGP can advertise separate multicast routes (SAFI=2). Inside a domain, OSPF or IS-IS can do this too. Most networks just use the unicast routes.

sections.title: Learning Where Sources Are
sections.content:
In Any Source Multicast (ASM), receivers want to receive from any source sending to a group, but the network must somehow learn which sources are active.

Source-Specific Multicast (SSM, RFC 4607) requires receivers to know the source address beforehand (from an out-of-band mechanism like a web page). No network-wide source discovery is needed. SSM is simpler but requires out-of-band discovery.

MSDP (Multicast Source Discovery Protocol, RFC 3618) connects multiple PIM-SM domains so sources in one domain can be discovered by RPs in other domains. It is the de-facto inter-domain ASM mechanism for IPv4. There is no intent to define MSDP for IPv6.

Embedded-RP (RFC 3956) encodes the RP's address into the multicast group address (IPv6 only). This eliminates the need for MSDP and allows multiple domains without a single global RP.
sections.eli5: If a receiver asks 'who is sending to this group?', routers need a way to answer. SSM says the receiver should know. MSDP lets RPs tell each other about sources. Embedded-RP builds the RP address into the group address.

sections.title: Configuring Rendezvous Points
sections.content:
In PIM-SM, a rendezvous point (RP) is the meeting point where sources register and where receivers' trees are rooted.

Static RP Configuration is the simplest: administrators manually configure which RP address each router uses for each multicast group. With anycast RP, multiple routers share the same RP address on their loopback interfaces, and unicast routing naturally picks the nearest one. This provides load sharing and redundancy without dynamic protocol overhead.

Auto-RP (Cisco proprietary) and BSR (Bootstrap Router, RFC 5059) are dynamic mechanisms that elect RPs and distribute group-to-RP mappings to all routers. They provide flexibility but add configuration and management complexity. With the widespread adoption of anycast RP, these mechanisms are less needed today.

Embedded-RP (IPv6 only) builds the RP address into the group address, eliminating configuration on non-RP routers.
sections.eli5: The rendezvous point is where sources announce themselves and receivers join. Admins can set one address manually (easiest), use anycast (multiple RPs with one address), or use Auto-RP or BSR to pick one dynamically.

sections.title: Redundancy and Flooding Reduction
sections.content:
Having a single RP is a single point of failure. Anycast RP with MSDP or PIM shares state between multiple RPs using either MSDP or PIM extensions, so if one RP fails, traffic continues. Bidirectional PIM eliminates the RP altogether, distributing the role across all routers.

On links where multicast traffic is flooded to every port (like Ethernet), IGMP snooping is the most widely deployed technique to reduce flooding. Switches snoop IGMP join messages from hosts and only flood multicast to ports with interested receivers. Full IGMPv3 and MLD snooping support is less common.

Other techniques include Cisco's CGMP and RGMP (proprietary), and IEEE 802.1D standards like GARP and GMRP (rarely deployed). IGMP proxying aggregates join messages when used with snooping on small routers.
sections.eli5: To avoid losing all multicast if the RP fails, you can run multiple RPs that share state. To avoid flooding the whole LAN with multicast, switches can snoop IGMP to only send to interested ports.
